frontmatter_description: Diagnose whether a disagreement requires bilateral concession to reach a mutually acceptable plan.
title: Negotiation, Concession, and Joint Plan
use_when: Use when the task asks who must adjust, concede, trade, or combine preferences to reach agreement.
Use when both sides retain some needs and the answer depends on how each side changes to form a joint solution.
Use when the key question is the shape of the compromise, not whether one speaker should persuade the other.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when only one person is changing their view, because that is persuasion, advice, or influence rather than negotiation.
Do not use when the scene is mainly about apology, repair, forgiveness, or easing hurt after harm.
Do not use when the main issue is hierarchy, authority, compliance, or deference instead of mutual adjustment.
Do not use when the question is about self-presentation, public image, or impression management rather than agreement design.
decision_variable: how both sides adjust to form a joint solution
trigger_checklist: Two parties have different preferences or demands.
Each side can give up something, trade something, or accept a partial match.
The answer depends on compromise rather than a single correct choice.
The scene asks for an agreed plan, split, or compromise outcome.
workflow: Identify each side's non-negotiable wants and flexible wants.
Check whether both sides can change terms without one side simply submitting.
Find the overlap or trade-off that satisfies enough of both sides.
Choose the option that is jointly acceptable, not merely persuasive or polite.

special_case.title: Concession without surrender
special_case.rule: A concession counts as negotiation only if the other side also changes terms, accepts a trade, or gains part of what they want.

worked_example.scene: Two coworkers want the same meeting room. One can move to a later time if the other shares equipment.
worked_example.question: What is the best social-cognitive interpretation?
worked_example.answer_logic: This is negotiation because both people adjust terms: one changes time, the other gives equipment access. The answer rests on bilateral concession, not one-sided persuasion.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to persuasion if one person is simply trying to make the other agree without reciprocal adjustment.
Exit to repair if the central issue is apology, blame, hurt, or restoring trust after a social violation.
Exit to power navigation if one side has authority and the main move is command, permission, escalation, or compliance.
Exit to self-presentation if the main issue is what image to project rather than what agreement to reach.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when a scene asks how two sides shape a mutually acceptable plan through compromise, trades, or concessions.
hard_boundary: Mutual adjustment is required; one-sided influence alone does not qualify.
The target is the structure of agreement, not the content of a final purchase, promise, or preference.
If apology or relationship repair is the main social work, route elsewhere.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not assume every disagreement is negotiation; many are persuasion or refusal.
Do not answer from fairness alone; the key is whether both sides change terms.
Do not confuse polite phrasing with actual concession.
common_failure_modes: Treating a compromise scene as simple persuasion.
Choosing the option that favors one side completely.
Missing a hidden trade-off that makes the plan jointly acceptable.
Confusing agreement-making with apology or reassurance.

minimal_pair.case: One friend says, 'Please come to my movie,' and keeps pushing until the other agrees.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This is not negotiation if only one side is trying to sway the other; it is persuasion.

minimal_pair.case: Two roommates split chores by each taking the task they dislike least.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This matches negotiation because both sides adjust preferences to reach a mutually acceptable division.

boundary_stress_test: If one person gives in and the other does not adjust at all, do not call it negotiation.
If the scene includes an apology but no trade or compromise, do not call it negotiation.
If the answer depends on rank, permission, or command, route away from this unit.
references.generalization_note: This unit generalizes to any social exchange where the diagnostic variable is reciprocal concession toward a shared plan, across friendships, work, family, and resource conflicts.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: Two people disagree, each can give something up, and the best answer is a compromise or trade that both can accept.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: One person argues hard to convince the other, but the other never changes their terms.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The issue is hurt feelings after a mistake, so the right move is apology or repair rather than negotiation.

notes: Keep the unit narrow: diagnose bilateral concession, not general agreement or conflict.
When in doubt, ask whether both minds are adapting; if not, this is probably not the right unit.
core_question: Find compromise, trades, and mutually acceptable plans under disagreement
